title: Senior Living Research Digest — Hearing Loss — June 2026
secondary_audience: families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

studies.title: Brain-training games may sharpen attention in older adults with hearing loss
studies.the_study: Researchers in Hong Kong tested a web-based, gamified program combining auditory and cognitive exercises in 60 community-dwelling older adults (mean age 68) with mild-to-moderate hearing loss. Over 12 weeks, the intervention group showed significant improvements in focused and divided attention compared to a waitlist control group. Participants also reported the training was enjoyable, easy to use, and boosted their self-awareness about hearing.
studies.why_it_matters: This pilot suggests that accessible, home-based digital training could help older adults maintain cognitive sharpness alongside hearing rehabilitation—potentially filling a gap where few such programs exist in Chinese languages.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have hearing loss, engaging brain-training apps designed for auditory challenges might help you stay mentally sharp. Ask your audiologist or healthcare provider about dual-task training programs—this study found them feasible and well-liked.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living activity directors could explore incorporating gamified auditory-cognitive programs into programming, especially for residents with hearing difficulties. Such tools may support both engagement and cognitive health.
studies.caveats: Small sample (N=60), single-center, waitlist control (no active comparison), short follow-up, conducted in Hong Kong (may not generalize broadly).

studies.title: Hearing aids linked to better memory and lower dementia risk, meta-analysis finds
studies.journal: Journal of Gerontology B: Psychological Sciences
studies.the_study: A systematic review and meta-analysis pooled data from 46 studies involving more than 231,000 older adults with hearing loss. Hearing aid use was associated with improved global cognition, memory, and executive function/attention, along with a 16% reduced risk of developing cognitive impairment. Benefits varied by age, sex, degree of hearing loss, and education level.
studies.why_it_matters: This is among the largest analyses to date linking hearing aid use with cognitive protection—strengthening the case that treating hearing loss may help preserve brain health in later life.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you've been putting off getting hearing aids, this research adds to evidence that using them may help protect your memory and thinking abilities over time. Talk to your doctor or audiologist about whether hearing aids could benefit you.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Families and caregivers should encourage loved ones with hearing loss to pursue hearing evaluation and, if appropriate, consistent hearing aid use. Senior living communities can support this by offering hearing screenings and helping residents maintain their devices.
studies.caveats: Observational studies predominate (cannot prove causation), heterogeneity across included studies, some subgroup effects inconsistent.

studies.title: Eating more flavonoid-rich foods tied to lower risk of hearing loss
studies.journal: Journal of Nutrition, Health and Aging
studies.the_study: Researchers followed nearly 56,000 UK Biobank participants without baseline hearing loss for an average of 11 years. Those with the highest intake of flavonoid-rich foods (berries, citrus, tea, red wine, dark chocolate) had a 16% lower risk of developing hearing loss compared to those with the lowest intake. Reduced inflammation, measured by C-reactive protein, partially explained the benefit.
studies.why_it_matters: Diet is a modifiable factor—this large study suggests that eating more colorful fruits, vegetables, and other flavonoid-rich foods may help protect hearing as you age.
studies.story_angle_primary: Adding berries, citrus fruits, tea, and dark leafy greens to your diet may support your hearing health. While more research is needed, these foods also benefit heart and brain health—so there's little downside to enjoying them regularly.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Dietitians and senior living dining services can promote flavonoid-rich menus as part of a hearing-healthy lifestyle. Families can encourage loved ones to choose colorful, plant-based foods at meals.
studies.caveats: Observational design (cannot establish causation), self-reported dietary data, UK population (may not generalize globally), relatively small effect size.

studies.title: Progressive hearing loss strongly linked to growing loneliness over time
studies.the_study: Using three waves of the Mexican Health and Aging Study (2015–2021), researchers tracked over 8,000 adults aged 60 and older. Progressive worsening of self-reported hearing within the same individual was significantly associated with increasing loneliness scores, independent of socioeconomic and health factors. Functional disability and chronic conditions also predicted loneliness.
studies.why_it_matters: This longitudinal design helps show that as hearing declines, loneliness grows—not just that people with hearing loss tend to be lonelier. Early intervention may help break this cycle.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you notice your hearing getting worse, pay attention to your social connections too. Addressing hearing loss early—through aids or other strategies—may help you stay connected and less isolated.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Caregivers and senior living staff should recognize that worsening hearing may predict increasing loneliness. Proactive communication support and social programming can help residents maintain meaningful relationships.
studies.caveats: Self-reported hearing (not audiometry), single-country sample (Mexico), observational (cannot prove causation).

studies.title: Depression risk rises with hearing loss across three countries
studies.the_study: Panel data from China, the U.S., and England (CHARLS, HRS, ELSA) showed a consistent pattern: among middle-aged and older adults, those reporting fair or poor hearing had significantly higher odds of depressive symptoms. The risk was roughly 50–65% higher for those with poor hearing compared to those with good hearing, even after adjusting for lifestyle and health factors.
studies.why_it_matters: This cross-cultural consistency underscores that hearing loss is a global risk factor for depression in later life—highlighting the need for routine mental health screening among those with hearing difficulties.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're struggling with hearing, know that it can also affect your mood. If you notice persistent sadness or low spirits, talk to your healthcare provider—addressing both hearing and emotional health together may help.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Clinicians, caregivers, and senior living professionals should screen for depression in residents or patients with hearing loss. Integrating hearing and mental health services can improve overall well-being.
studies.caveats: Self-reported hearing and depression, observational design, cross-sectional elements within panel structure.

studies.title: Hearing loss linked to higher dementia and Alzheimer's burden worldwide
studies.the_study: Analyzing Global Burden of Disease data from 1990–2021, researchers found that while age-related hearing loss burden remained relatively stable, Alzheimer's disease incidence and disability-adjusted life-years increased steadily, especially among women and older age groups. A positive cross-national correlation was observed between hearing loss prevalence and Alzheimer's burden, reflecting shared demographic pressures.
studies.why_it_matters: The co-occurrence of hearing loss and dementia at the population level suggests coordinated public health planning is needed—especially as both conditions are projected to rise through 2040.
studies.story_angle_primary: Protecting your hearing may be one piece of a larger puzzle for brain health. Staying proactive about hearing checkups and cognitive screenings can help you and your doctor catch problems early.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Policymakers and senior care administrators should consider integrating hearing and cognitive health programs, particularly in regions with rapidly aging populations.
studies.caveats: Ecological/population-level data (not individual-level causation), relies on reported statistics which may vary by country, projections are estimates.

studies.title: Childhood adversity tied to poorer hearing, vision, and dual sensory loss in later life
studies.journal: Journal of Gerontology B: Psychological Sciences
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed data from China's CHARLS cohort to examine how adverse childhood experiences (ACEs)—such as physical abuse, parental loss, and household violence—relate to sensory loss trajectories in later life. Greater ACE exposure was associated with worse hearing, vision, and dual sensory loss trajectories. Physical abuse and household violence were identified as the most central risk factors.
studies.why_it_matters: This life-course perspective shows that early trauma may have lasting effects on sensory health decades later, pointing to the importance of trauma-informed care for older adults.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you experienced difficult circumstances in childhood, your risk for hearing or vision problems later in life may be somewhat higher. Regular checkups can help catch changes early.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Healthcare providers and senior living staff should consider trauma history when assessing sensory health and provide compassionate, trauma-informed support.
studies.caveats: Observational, self-reported ACEs (recall bias possible), Chinese population (may not generalize globally).

studies.title: Hearing loss adversely affects adaptation to aging—but not nursing home adjustment
studies.the_study: Researchers in Turkey compared 65 nursing home residents—34 with hearing loss and 31 with normal hearing. Those with hearing loss scored significantly worse on measures of adaptation to aging (especially in roles, self-actualization, and physiological functioning), but nursing home adjustment scores did not differ between groups. Perceived health was the strongest predictor of aging adaptation.
studies.why_it_matters: While hearing loss complicates the process of adapting to aging, it does not necessarily prevent successful adjustment to nursing home life—suggesting that supportive environments and positive health perceptions can help.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have hearing loss, you may face extra challenges adapting to aging, but that doesn't mean you can't thrive in a nursing home. Seek support for your hearing needs and focus on what makes you feel healthy and engaged.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Nursing home staff should address hearing loss proactively, but also recognize that fostering positive health perceptions and providing individualized support can help residents adapt well regardless of hearing status.
studies.caveats: Small sample (N=65), single-site, cross-sectional design.

studies.title: Wearing hearing aids at least 8 hours daily linked to lower frailty risk
studies.the_study: A cross-sectional survey of 332 older adults (mean age 81) with hearing loss in Japan found that those who wore their hearing aids less than 8 hours per day had more than three times the odds of being frail compared to those who wore them 8–12 hours daily. Other factors like fitting quality and frequency of use were also assessed.
studies.why_it_matters: Consistent hearing aid use appears to matter—not just having devices, but wearing them throughout the day may help protect against frailty.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have hearing aids, try to wear them throughout your waking hours—not just occasionally. This study suggests that consistent use may help you stay stronger and more independent.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Audiologists, caregivers, and senior living staff should encourage and monitor daily hearing aid use, helping residents troubleshoot barriers to consistent wear.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional (cannot prove causation), self-reported use, single-country sample (Japan).

studies.title: Emotional and financial support help older adults keep using their hearing aids
studies.the_study: In a cohort of 355 Chilean adults aged 65–85 who received hearing aids through a public program, 21.7% abandoned them. Those who received financial assistance for device maintenance and had higher emotional support scores were significantly less likely to abandon their hearing aids. Household composition and contact frequency with close relatives also affected outcomes.
studies.why_it_matters: Hearing aids only help if people use them—family support and help with costs can make the difference between consistent use and abandonment.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're struggling with your hearing aids, reach out to family or friends for encouragement and practical help. Financial assistance programs may also be available to help cover maintenance costs.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Families should stay involved in a loved one's hearing care journey—offering emotional support and helping with device upkeep. Senior living communities can connect residents with social and financial resources to support hearing aid use.
studies.caveats: Single-country sample (Chile), observational design, public policy context may differ elsewhere.

studies.title: Older adults with hearing loss may need to advocate for themselves in healthcare settings
studies.the_study: A qualitative pilot study of 15 older adults with hearing loss and chronic illness (plus their partners) found that participants routinely had to advocate for themselves to have their hearing loss acknowledged in healthcare encounters. Many feared missing important information or experiencing misunderstandings because providers rarely asked about or accommodated their hearing needs.
studies.why_it_matters: The burden of ensuring communication access currently falls on patients—this study calls for healthcare systems to proactively identify and accommodate hearing loss.
studies.story_angle_primary: Don't hesitate to tell your healthcare providers about your hearing loss and ask for accommodations—such as facing you directly, speaking clearly, or providing written instructions. You have the right to understand your care.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Healthcare systems and senior living facilities should routinely screen for and document hearing loss, then adjust communication practices accordingly—rather than relying on patients to self-advocate every time.
studies.caveats: Small qualitative sample (N=15), pilot study, may not generalize to all healthcare contexts.

studies.title: Cognitive impairment common among audiology clinic patients—many unaware
studies.the_study: Researchers compared 83 patients from an audiological clinic to 39 community-dwelling older adults on cognitive tests. Clinic patients performed significantly worse on measures of processing speed, working memory, executive function, memory, and visuoconstruction. Between 10–15% of clinic patients scored in the impaired range, and nearly half of those with impairment reported no memory problems.
studies.why_it_matters: Many older adults seeking hearing care may also have undetected cognitive difficulties—routine cognitive screening in audiology settings could help identify those who need further evaluation.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're getting your hearing checked, consider asking about a brief cognitive screening as well. Some memory or thinking changes may go unnoticed, and catching them early can help you get the right support.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Audiologists and hearing care providers should consider incorporating simple cognitive screens into routine practice, as many patients may not recognize or report cognitive concerns.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, single clinic, relatively small sample, Danish population.

studies.title: Worse hearing linked to poorer cognition and quality of life in older adults
studies.the_study: In a study of 60 Serbian adults aged 60 and older (40 with presbycusis, 20 with normal/mild hearing loss), worse hearing thresholds were strongly correlated with poorer scores on the MMSE and MoCA cognitive screens. Most participants with hearing loss scored in the range suggestive of cognitive impairment, and 90% reported reduced hearing-related quality of life.
studies.why_it_matters: The connection between hearing loss and cognitive screening performance reinforces the case for early hearing assessment and intervention in older adults.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have hearing loss, know that it can affect how you perform on memory and thinking tests—and possibly your daily quality of life. Getting your hearing checked and treated may support your overall brain health.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Clinicians should interpret cognitive screening results in the context of hearing status and consider referring for hearing evaluation when appropriate.
studies.caveats: Small sample (N=60), single-center, cross-sectional, self-reported duration of hearing loss.

studies.title: Hearing loss predicts faster cognitive decline over 24 years
studies.the_study: Using 24 years of data from the Health and Retirement Study (N=7,598), researchers found that incident hearing loss was associated with both an acute drop and an accelerated ongoing decline in global cognition, memory, orientation, and calculation. The effects were observed immediately at hearing loss onset and continued over time.
studies.why_it_matters: This long-term longitudinal evidence strengthens the link between hearing loss and cognitive decline, suggesting that addressing hearing loss early could help slow cognitive aging.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you notice your hearing changing, don't delay—getting it checked and treated may help protect your memory and thinking abilities over the years ahead.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Primary care providers and senior living staff should prioritize hearing assessments as part of routine health monitoring, especially for those showing early cognitive changes.
studies.caveats: Observational (cannot prove causation), self-reported hearing loss, U.S. population.

studies.title: Hearing loss in cognitively frail elders predicts faster progression to dementia
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed data from 4,805 Chinese adults aged 65 and older over seven years. Cognitive impairment was more strongly associated with frailty progression than the reverse. Among those already frail, hearing loss, poor sleep, and illiteracy were significant predictors of cognitive decline.
studies.why_it_matters: For older adults already vulnerable to frailty, addressing hearing loss and sleep problems may help delay cognitive decline.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're experiencing both physical frailty and hearing difficulties, treating your hearing may help protect your thinking abilities. Talk to your doctor about a comprehensive evaluation.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Geriatricians and senior care teams should target modifiable risk factors—hearing loss, sleep disturbance—in frail older adults to help slow cognitive decline.
studies.caveats: Observational, self-reported measures, Chinese population.

studies.title: Four distinct depression trajectories identified among older adults with hearing loss
studies.the_study: Using four waves of CHARLS data (2011–2018), researchers identified four depressive symptom trajectories among 1,556 older Chinese adults with hearing loss: increasing, severe-stable, no symptoms, and decreasing. Female sex, poor self-rated health, and low life satisfaction predicted worse trajectories; longer sleep and higher functional ability were protective.
studies.why_it_matters: Not all older adults with hearing loss experience the same mental health course—identifying high-risk subgroups can help target interventions.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have hearing loss and notice persistent sadness, know that your experience may follow a distinct pattern. Good sleep, staying active, and seeking support can help improve your outlook.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Screening for depression in those with hearing loss should consider psychosocial factors like life satisfaction and functional ability to identify those most at risk.
studies.caveats: Observational, self-reported measures, Chinese population.

studies.title: Hearing loss tied to more sitting, but not less physical activity
studies.journal: Journal of Gerontology A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
studies.the_study: In a nationally representative sample of 3,512 Chilean adults aged 40 and older, self-reported hearing loss was associated with nearly double the odds of prolonged sedentary behavior (sitting 8+ hours/day), but was not associated with overall physical activity levels or domain-specific activity at work, transport, or leisure.
studies.why_it_matters: Hearing loss may not stop people from being active, but it may lead to more sitting—a risk factor for chronic disease. Reducing sedentary time could be a key intervention target.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have hearing loss, you may find yourself sitting more than you realize. Try to break up long periods of sitting with short walks or stretches—even if your overall activity level is fine.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living programs should encourage movement breaks and reduce prolonged sitting among residents with hearing loss, even if they participate in regular activities.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, self-reported hearing and activity, Chilean population.

studies.title: Recognizing and managing hearing loss in care homes: a nursing overview
studies.the_study: This clinical review provides guidance for nurses and care home staff on recognizing and managing hearing loss in older adults. It covers auditory anatomy, types and causes of hearing loss, adverse effects (falls, cognitive decline), and a best-practice checklist for care home settings.
studies.why_it_matters: Hearing loss is common but often overlooked in care homes—practical guidance for staff can improve residents' safety, communication, and quality of life.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you live in a care home and struggle to hear, let staff know so they can help you access support and accommodations. You deserve clear communication.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Nursing staff and care home managers should use evidence-based checklists to screen for, document, and manage hearing loss among residents, reducing risks of falls and cognitive decline.
studies.caveats: Clinical overview/guidance (not original research), based on existing literature.

studies.title: Short-term hearing aid use changes brain responses to speech in noise
studies.the_study: Using magnetoencephalography, researchers found that after just three months of regular hearing aid use, first-time users with age-related hearing loss showed reduced auditory cortical activity when listening to speech in noise. Individual improvements in speech-in-noise performance were linked to reductions in left-hemisphere brain activity.
studies.why_it_matters: This neuroimaging study provides evidence that the brain can adapt quickly to hearing aids—potentially making speech understanding easier with consistent use.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you're new to hearing aids, give them time—your brain may adapt within just a few months, making it easier to understand conversations, especially in noisy places.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Audiologists and caregivers should encourage consistent hearing aid use and reassure new users that brain adaptation can happen relatively quickly.
studies.caveats: Small sample, preliminary study, short follow-up (3 months), single-center.

studies.title: Music enjoyment preserved despite hearing loss—with training and adaptation
studies.the_study: In a mixed-methods study of 85 older adults (aged 60+) across the hearing spectrum, worse hearing loss was associated with reduced music perception and listening frequency, but not with overall music reward or active participation. Musical training and adaptive strategies helped preserve enjoyment, often through emotional connections like nostalgia.
studies.why_it_matters: Music remains a source of joy and meaning for many older adults with hearing loss—especially those with musical backgrounds who adapt their listening habits.
studies.story_angle_primary: If hearing loss has changed how you experience music, don't give up. Try new strategies—like adjusting volume, using headphones, or focusing on favorite genres—and lean into the emotional memories music brings you.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Music therapists and senior living activity coordinators should encourage music engagement for residents with hearing loss, emphasizing personalized approaches and emotional connection over perfect perception.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, self-reported musical engagement, cochlear implant users excluded from quantitative analysis.

studies.title: Hearing loss associated with multiple aging-related health problems
studies.the_study: In a cohort of 545 Chinese adults (mean age 65, 69% women), hearing loss was significantly associated with poorer cognitive function, reduced ability to perform daily activities, nutritional risk, and sarcopenia. Moderate or higher hearing loss showed the strongest associations.
studies.why_it_matters: Hearing loss doesn't occur in isolation—it clusters with other health challenges, making comprehensive geriatric assessment essential.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have hearing loss, ask your doctor to also check your nutrition, strength, and thinking abilities. Addressing all of these together can help you stay independent longer.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Geriatricians and care teams should view hearing loss as a signal to assess multiple health domains, not just auditory function.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, single-center, Chinese population, modest sample size.

studies.title: Arthritis linked to higher risk of hearing and vision loss over time
studies.the_study: Analyzing 5,187 Chinese older adults over seven years, researchers found that those with arthritis had significantly higher incidence of hearing loss, vision loss, and dual sensory loss, with accelerated deterioration over time compared to those without arthritis.
studies.why_it_matters: Arthritis may be a warning sign for sensory decline—early and ongoing screening for hearing and vision in arthritis patients could help catch problems sooner.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you have arthritis, pay extra attention to your hearing and vision. Ask your doctor about regular screenings, as you may be at higher risk for sensory changes.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Rheumatologists, primary care providers, and senior living health staff should include sensory assessments as part of routine care for arthritis patients.
studies.caveats: Observational, self-reported arthritis and sensory function, Chinese population.

studies.title: Moderate-to-severe hearing loss affects more than a quarter of older Chinese adults—especially women
studies.the_study: In a cross-sectional study of 2,465 older Chinese adults, 26.8% had moderate-to-severe speech-frequency hearing loss, 19.1% had low-frequency loss, and 66.8% had high-frequency loss. Women showed a greater increase in hearing loss prevalence with age compared to men, suggesting possible sex-specific factors.
studies.why_it_matters: The high prevalence of significant hearing loss—especially among older women—highlights the need for routine screening and investigation into sex differences, including the potential role of menopause.
studies.story_angle_primary: Hearing loss is common and may progress faster in women as they age. Regular hearing checkups can help catch changes early, so ask your doctor about screening.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Senior living communities and health systems should prioritize hearing assessments for older women and consider sex-specific factors in care planning.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, Chinese population, self-reported and audiometric data combined.

studies.title: Positive views of aging may encourage earlier help-seeking for hearing loss
studies.the_study: In 503 adults (mean age 64, 69% female) with at least some hearing difficulty, awareness of age-related losses was associated with formal help-seeking and hearing aid use. Among older adults, a positive, gain-focused view of aging was linked to greater informal help-seeking (talking to friends and family about hearing concerns).
studies.why_it_matters: How people perceive their own aging may influence whether and when they seek help for hearing loss—suggesting that promoting positive aging attitudes could support earlier intervention.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you notice hearing changes, don't dismiss them as "just getting old." Talking to friends, family, or a healthcare provider early can help you get the support you need—and a positive outlook on aging may make it easier to take that step.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Clinicians and senior living staff can encourage help-seeking by normalizing age-related changes and fostering positive conversations about aging and hearing health.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional, self-reported hearing and perceptions, app-based sample (may not generalize).

studies.title: Preventing hearing loss could avert tens of thousands of new dementia cases annually in the U.S.
studies.journal: Journal of Gerontology A: Biological Sciences and Medical Sciences
studies.the_study: Using a validated microsimulation model, researchers estimated that about 141,000 new dementia cases in 2022 among U.S. adults over 60 could be attributed to hearing loss. Hearing loss and associated dementia reduced lifetime quality-adjusted life-years by 1.4–1.7 years. The model projects that preventing hearing loss could substantially reduce new dementia cases.
studies.why_it_matters: This modeling study quantifies the potential public health impact of hearing loss on dementia, strengthening the case for prioritizing hearing health in dementia prevention strategies.
studies.story_angle_primary: Protecting your hearing may help protect your brain. If you haven't had a hearing test recently, consider scheduling one—catching and treating hearing loss early could make a difference.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Public health officials and senior care organizations should invest in hearing loss prevention and treatment as part of dementia risk reduction efforts.
studies.caveats: Modeling study (not direct observation), relies on assumptions and estimates, U.S. population.

studies.title: Online geriatric screening tool successfully identifies hearing loss and other syndromes in primary care
studies.the_study: In a cross-sectional study of 374 older Thai adults (mean age 76), an online self-administered screening tool based on the WHO ICOPE framework detected high rates of geriatric syndromes, including hearing loss (associated with older age). fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Senior Living Research Digest — June 2026
**Checked:** 2026-06-28 | **Studies reviewed:** 40
**Primary audience:** older adults and seniors | **Secondary audience:** families, caregivers, and senior living professionals

---

# Fact-Check Report

## Study 1: Brain-training games may sharpen attention in older adults with hearing loss
**PMID:** 42302249 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract. The digest accurately reports the sample size (N=60), population (community-dwelling older adults with mild-to-moderate hearing loss), mean age (67.65 rounded to 68), Hong Kong location, 12-week intervention, and key findings on focused and divided attention improvements. The caveats appropriately note limitations.

---

## Study 2: Hearing aids linked to better memory and lower dementia risk, meta-analysis finds
**PMID:** 41803081 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Slight misstatement of risk reduction metric** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "along with a 16% reduced risk of developing cognitive impairment"
- **Abstract says:** "along with a decreased risk of cognitive impairment (RR = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.80, 0.88)"
- **Problem:** The digest correctly calculated 16% from RR=0.84, but the abstract reports this as "relative risk" not "risk," a minor terminological distinction that doesn't materially affect accuracy.
- **Suggested fix:** No change needed; calculation is correct.

No other issues. Sample size (231,565), 46 studies, and key findings are accurate.

---

## Study 3: Eating more flavonoid-rich foods tied to lower risk of hearing loss
**PMID:** 42235109 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Food examples include item not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Those with the highest intake of flavonoid-rich foods (berries, citrus, tea, red wine, dark chocolate)"
- **Abstract says:** "FDS was calculated from flavonoid-rich food intake" — no specific foods listed
- **Problem:** The digest lists specific foods (berries, citrus, tea, red wine, dark chocolate) that are not mentioned in the abstract. While these are plausible flavonoid sources, they cannot be verified from the abstract alone.
- **Suggested fix:** "Those with the highest intake of flavonoid-rich foods had a 16% lower risk..." (remove specific food examples, or flag as inferred from general knowledge)

**Issue B. Follow-up duration slightly imprecise** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "an average of 11 years"
- **Abstract says:** "613,590 person-years of follow-up" for 55,859 participants (≈11 years average)
- **Problem:** The calculation is correct but the abstract doesn't state "11 years" explicitly.
- **Suggested fix:** No change strictly necessary; calculation is reasonable.

---

## Study 4: Progressive hearing loss strongly linked to growing loneliness over time
**PMID:** 42065922 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The digest accurately reports the data source (Mexican Health and Aging Study 2015-2021), longitudinal design, within-individual association, and key findings. The sample size is stated as "over 8,000" which is consistent with a three-wave study of adults 60+, though the exact N isn't specified in the abstract.

---

## Study 5: Depression risk rises with hearing loss across three countries
**PMID:** 42119796 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Effect size range slightly imprecise** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The risk was roughly 50–65% higher for those with poor hearing"
- **Abstract says:** OR values of 1.52, 1.64, and 1.55 for poor hearing across the three cohorts
- **Problem:** 1.52-1.64 represents 52-64% higher odds, not "50-65%." This is a minor rounding difference.
- **Suggested fix:** "The risk was roughly 52–64% higher" or keep as approximate.

No other issues. Study design, countries, and key findings are accurate.

---

## Study 6: Hearing loss linked to higher dementia and Alzheimer's burden worldwide
**PMID:** 41722206 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The digest accurately describes this as a Global Burden of Disease analysis (1990-2021), notes the ecological/population-level correlation between ARHL and Alzheimer's burden, and appropriately frames this as "co-occurrence" rather than causation. Projections to 2040 are correctly mentioned.

---

## Study 7: Childhood adversity tied to poorer hearing, vision, and dual sensory loss in later life
**PMID:** 41808451 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The digest accurately reports the CHARLS data source, the association between ACEs and sensory loss trajectories, and the identification of physical abuse and household violence as central risk factors. Framing is appropriately observational.

---

## Study 8: Hearing loss adversely affects adaptation to aging—but not nursing home adjustment
**PMID:** 41558452 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Sample size (N=65, 34 with hearing loss, 31 with normal hearing), Turkish setting, key findings on ASADE subscales, and the null finding on NHAS are all accurate. The finding that perceived health was the strongest predictor of aging adaptation is correctly reported.

---

## Study 9: Wearing hearing aids at least 8 hours daily linked to lower frailty risk
**PMID:** 41942921 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Sample size (N=332), mean age (81.30, rounded to 81), Japan setting, and the key finding (OR 3.32 for <8 hours vs. 8-12 hours) are accurate. The digest correctly frames the comparison group as 8-12 hours daily use.

---
